new_statements.rule_in_words: In Collins' own field transcription of Masiwang (Kota Baru), words bear penultimate stress by default; the few Masiwang items he marks otherwise are mostly final-stressed (ahás 'stir', mumáh 'yawn', hosúf 'blow', aisó 'you sg', mahó/masó 'that'; also mehéi 'this', eéyi 'no', ilyówas 'star', yatáua 'where'). This is a wordlist notation convention applied to six East Seram languages, not an analytic phonological statement, but it is first-hand and unambiguously about Masiwang.
new_statements.exceptions: Only implicitly, via accent marks on individual Masiwang forms in the 200-item list (roughly ten of ~200 items, mostly final stress, several of them pronouns/demonstratives).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms in an elicited 200-word comparative list; word-level transcription convention; no statement about phrase stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Collins 1986) is Collins' own transcription of Masiwang as spoken at Kota Baru (with a few items from Dawang), north-west of the Masiwang river estuary, East Seram = masi1266 proper ('formerly called Bonfia', Collins 1986:125). CAUTION on the other candidate: Tauern 1931 (Anthropos 26:128-130) gives an explicit penult rule for a 'Bonfia-Sprache', but his section is headed 'Liambata-Dialekt der Alfuren von Ostseran'; Collins 1986:125 lists Liambata as a Seti-speaking village (and n.2 notes Tauern supplied Stresemann with 'information about Liambata'), Glottolog gives 'Liambata-Kobi' as an alternate name of Liana-Seti, and Tauern's Bonfia lexicon/pronouns match Collins' Seti column rather than his Masiwang column. Tauern's 'Bonfia' statement therefore most likely belongs to Liana-Seti (lian1255, already catalogued from the same article's Uhei-Kahlakim section) and should NOT be filed under masi1266.

sources.note: Subgrouping paper based on Collins' own 1977-79 fieldwork; no phonology section, but the Appendix (p.141) states the transcription convention for the 200-item comparative list of six languages incl. Masiwang (Kota Baru): 'stress is penultimate unless otherwise marked'. In the Masiwang column (pp.142-145) only a handful of forms carry a stress mark, mostly final: ahás 'stir', mumáh 'yawn', hosúf 'blow', aisó 'you (sg)', mahó/masó 'that', mehéi 'this', eéyi 'no'; also ilyówas 'star', yatáua 'where'. Also p.125: Masiwang 'formerly called Bonfia', known until then only from Le Cocq d'Armandville…
